prompt: A car coasts in neutral from the top of a hill to the bottom and arrives more slowly than the conservation of mechanical energy predicts. A learner concludes that some of the energy "was destroyed by friction". Evaluate this conclusion.
answer: The conclusion is wrong. Mechanical energy was not conserved, and no energy was destroyed.
explanation: The principle of conservation of MECHANICAL energy applies only when the only forces doing work are conservative ones such as gravity. Friction and air resistance are not conservative, so on a real hill the sum of kinetic and gravitational potential energy does fall — the learner's measurement is sound. What happened to that energy is transfer, not destruction: friction between the tyres, brakes and axles, and drag against the air, raise the internal energy of the car, the road surface and the surrounding air, which end up very slightly warmer, and a little is carried away as sound. Add those to the account and the total is exactly what it was at the top. Conservation of ENERGY has no exceptions; conservation of MECHANICAL energy has a stated condition, and this hill does not meet it.

prompt: A learner states that a ball thrown vertically upward has its maximum kinetic energy at the highest point of its flight, "because that is where it has climbed the furthest and so has the most energy". Evaluate this claim.
answer: The claim is exactly inverted. The highest point is where kinetic energy is at a MINIMUM — zero — and potential energy at a maximum.
explanation: Kinetic energy is Ek = ½mv², so it depends on speed alone. A ball thrown upward slows continuously as gravity acts against its motion, reaching v = 0 at the highest point, so Ek = 0 there. Gravitational potential energy is Ep = mgh and depends on height, so it is greatest at exactly the same instant. The learner has conflated "the most energy" with "the most kinetic energy": the TOTAL mechanical energy is indeed unchanged throughout the flight in the absence of air resistance, which is probably the fact being half-remembered, and its division between the two forms swings completely from one end of the motion to the other. At launch it is all kinetic; at the top it is all potential; on return to the hand it is all kinetic again, at the original speed.

prompt: A 0.6 kg ball is thrown vertically upward. A learner argues that at the highest point the ball has no energy at all, "because it has stopped moving, and a stationary object has no energy". Evaluate this claim.
answer: The claim is wrong. The ball's kinetic energy is zero there; its total mechanical energy is unchanged and is entirely potential.
explanation: Stopping removes kinetic energy, not energy. At the highest point v = 0, so Ek = ½mv² = 0 — the learner has that part right. But the ball is now at its greatest height, so Ep = mgh is at its largest, and the total is the same as it was at launch. The decisive evidence is what happens next: an object with no energy has no way to do anything, and this ball accelerates back down and arrives with exactly the kinetic energy it was thrown with. That returning kinetic energy has to have been stored somewhere, and the store is its position in the gravitational field. Treating "at rest" as "without energy" would also make a boulder poised at the top of a cliff harmless.

prompt: Two balls, one of 0.4 kg and one of 1.2 kg, are thrown vertically upward at the same initial speed. A learner predicts the heavier ball will rise higher, "because it has more energy when it leaves the hand". Evaluate this claim, ignoring air resistance.
answer: The claim is wrong. Both rise to exactly the same height, because the extra energy is matched by the extra weight it has to lift.
explanation: The heavier ball does leave the hand with more kinetic energy — three times as much, since Ek = ½mv² and the speed is the same. But it also needs more energy to gain each metre of height, because Ep = mgh rises three times as fast for it too. Setting ½mv² = mgh, the mass cancels from both sides and h = v² ÷ 2g, which contains no m at all: at 10 m·s⁻¹ both reach 5.1 m. The learner has correctly identified one side of the comparison and not checked the other, which is the commonest way a Level 4 prediction goes wrong. This is the same cancellation that makes all objects fall at the same rate in a vacuum, and air resistance — deliberately excluded here — is what makes the everyday world seem to disagree.

prompt: A learner argues that mechanical energy must be conserved for a falling ball even when air resistance acts, "because energy is always conserved, and that is a law". Evaluate this claim.
answer: The law cited is correct and the wrong law has been cited. Total energy is always conserved; MECHANICAL energy is conserved only under a condition this situation breaks.
explanation: Two different statements are being run together. Conservation of total energy holds without exception: energy can be transferred and converted but not created or destroyed. Conservation of mechanical energy is a narrower and conditional result — the sum Ek + Ep stays constant only when the work done by non-conservative forces is zero. Air resistance is a non-conservative force, and it does negative work on the falling ball throughout, so Ek + Ep decreases measurably: the ball lands slower than √(2gh) predicts, and eventually reaches a terminal velocity at which Ek stops rising altogether while Ep goes on falling. The missing energy is in the warmed air and the warmed ball. Quoting a broad law to override a narrow one whose conditions are not met is the error, and it is why the mechanical-energy statement is always taught with its condition attached.

prompt: A learner claims that a ball thrown vertically upward returns to the thrower's hand faster than it left, "because gravity has had the whole flight to act on it". Evaluate this claim, ignoring air resistance.
answer: The claim is wrong. It returns at exactly the speed it left at, because the flight is symmetrical.
explanation: Gravity acts for the whole flight, which is true, and it acts in opposite senses over the two halves: against the motion while the ball rises, removing kinetic energy, and with the motion while it falls, restoring exactly the same amount. The ball leaves the hand at height h with mechanical energy ½mv², and it returns to the same height, so its potential energy is the same and therefore so is its kinetic energy — which fixes the speed. The equations agree: the ball rises for v ÷ g and falls for v ÷ g, reaching the launch height with speed v downward. Air resistance, which this question excludes, would make the return speed LOWER than the launch speed, not higher, since it opposes the motion in both directions. So no version of the physics supports the learner's conclusion.

prompt: A hiker argues that taking a long zigzag path up a hill requires more energy against gravity than climbing straight up, "because you walk much further". Evaluate the hiker's reasoning, treating the walking itself as frictionless.
answer: The work done against GRAVITY is identical, because gravitational potential energy depends only on the change in height.
explanation: Ep = mgh contains the vertical height and nothing else — not the distance walked, not the route, not the steepness. Gravity is a conservative force, which means precisely that the work done against it between two points is independent of the path taken; a 70 kg hiker climbing 400 m does 70 × 9.8 × 400 ≈ 274 kJ against gravity by any route. On the zigzag, the force needed at each step is smaller because the slope is gentler, and the distance is correspondingly longer, and the product is unchanged. Real hikers are right that the zigzag is easier and wrong about why: it is easier because it demands less force at any moment, not less energy overall. Outside this question's frictionless idealisation the longer path does cost extra in friction and in the inefficiency of human muscle, which is a separate account from the work against gravity.

prompt: Two frictionless slides drop through the same height, one short and steep and one long and gentle. A learner predicts that a child on the gentle slide arrives faster, "because there is more time for gravity to accelerate them". Evaluate this claim.
answer: The claim is wrong. Both arrive at the same SPEED; the gentle slide simply takes longer to get there.
explanation: Conservation of mechanical energy settles it without any reference to the shape of the slide: mgh converts entirely to ½mv², the mass cancels, and v = √(2gh) depends only on the height dropped. Both slides drop the same height, so both give the same arrival speed. The learner is right that the journey lasts longer on the gentle slide, and has assumed that longer acceleration means a greater final speed — which would hold only if the acceleration were the same on both. It is not: the component of gravity along a gentle slope is smaller, so the child accelerates more slowly for longer, and the two effects cancel exactly. Time and final speed are being confused, and separating them is the whole of this question.

prompt: A road safety pamphlet states that driving at 60 km·h⁻¹ instead of 30 km·h⁻¹ "doubles the energy in a crash". Evaluate this claim.
answer: The claim badly understates the danger. Doubling the speed QUADRUPLES the kinetic energy, because Ek depends on v².
explanation: Ek = ½mv², so kinetic energy rises with the SQUARE of the speed: doubling v multiplies Ek by four, not two. A 1 200 kg car at 30 km·h⁻¹ (8.33 m·s⁻¹) carries about 42 kJ; at 60 km·h⁻¹ (16.7 m·s⁻¹) it carries about 167 kJ. All of that has to be dissipated in the crash, by the crumpling of the vehicle and by whatever it strikes. The same square law governs braking distance, which also quadruples for a given deceleration, so a driver at double the speed both takes four times the distance to stop and arrives with four times the energy if they cannot. The pamphlet's error is the natural one of assuming energy scales like speed, and it makes the message far less alarming than the physics warrants.
